analysis.one_liner: Forces the government to reissue and lock in the environmental approval for the Resolution Copper mine in Arizona.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Natural Resources Committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Secretary of Agriculture to reissue, within 90 days, the final environmental impact statement for the Resolution Copper mine and land exchange in Arizona — a statement the Forest Service withdrew on March 5, 2021. It would also bar the Secretary from withdrawing that statement again, and declare that the reissued document automatically satisfies the National Environmental Policy Act, the law that normally requires a full environmental review before major federal land decisions. In effect, Congress would have finished the environmental review by statute and locked in the approval the mine needed.
analysis.who_benefits: The company behind the Resolution Copper Project — a joint venture of the mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP — would gain the most. The bill would force the government to revive the environmental approval the project needs within 90 days and lock it in place, clearing the way for a land exchange that hands federal land, including a site sacred to Apache tribes, to the mining venture. Manufacturers that use copper would also gain a new domestic supply source.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would give the Resolution Copper Project the environmental sign-off it lost when the Forest Service withdrew its final impact statement in March 2021, and would do so on a 90-day deadline.

It would go further than restoring the review: the Secretary could never withdraw the statement again, and the document would be deemed by law to satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act, ending any further environmental challenge on those grounds.

Supporters of domestic mining would point to the project's purpose — a large new domestic copper supply for wiring, electronics, and electric vehicles — as a national benefit the review was holding up.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the costs would fall on Apache tribes and other local communities for whom the land involved in the exchange is sacred, and on the public more broadly, because the bill would shortcut the environmental review process that normally evaluates a project of this scale before it proceeds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tribes and the public near the mine

drawbacks.text: The bill would legislate the conclusion of an environmental review rather than let the review be done: by declaring the reissued statement compliant with NEPA and forbidding its withdrawal, it would remove the public's normal chance to challenge or revisit the analysis before one of the largest copper mines in the country proceeds.

The statement it would revive had already been withdrawn once by the agency responsible for it, and the bill would take away the agency's authority to make that judgment again — substituting a congressional mandate for the professional review process.

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill does nothing to fix whatever defect led the Forest Service to pull the statement in the first place; it simply orders the same document reissued and immunized.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — a faster path to domestic copper production — would accrue mainly to a single foreign-owned mining venture, while its cost would be borne by tribes and the public, who would lose the opportunity to contest or supplement the environmental analysis of a project affecting sacred land and major water resources. The bill's central design flaw is that it answers an environmental question by statute rather than by study: it does not cure the problem that led to the withdrawal, it only declares the document valid. On balance, the bill's value to ordinary people is speculative and its cost to public process is concrete.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Lesko introduced the bill on May 11, 2022, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day and received no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of fast-tracking the mine came out ahead: the Forest Service kept its discretion, no land exchange approval was forced through by statute, and the project remained subject to the normal environmental process. The mining venture gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tribes and groups opposing the mine

for.name: Rep. Debbie Lesko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or action on the bill after it was referred on May 11, 2022

against.name: U.S. Forest Service
against.role: Federal land agency under the Department of Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Withdrew the final environmental impact statement for the Resolution Copper project on March 5, 2021 — the decision this bill sought to overturn

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no party-line split can be measured.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Rio Tinto–BHP Resolution Copper venture)
industries.note: The bill would hand the venture the one approval it lacked — a final environmental impact statement — within 90 days and make it unrevocable, bypassing further NEPA review. The land exchange at issue would convey federal land, including a site sacred to Apache tribes, to the mining company.
A new domestic copper mine would expand supply of a metal used in wiring, electronics, and electric vehicles, lowering a cost input for these manufacturers. Their gain is indirect and long-term.
